examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Desktop Foundations Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam checks foundational Tableau Desktop skills, such as connecting to data, creating views, using common calculations, and building dashboards. Salesforce describes the audience as people with foundational skills and recommends at least three months of experience using Tableau Desktop.
bullets: Format: The official guide lists 40 scored multiple-choice or multiple-select questions, up to five unscored questions, and 70 minutes.
48% to pass, which is 20 correct answers out of 40.
Core skills: Prepare data, create views, use filters and calculations, and share findings through dashboards.
Practice: Build and explore views in Tableau Desktop, then check each skill against the current exam outline.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice connecting to data, choosing a view, adding filters, creating a simple calculation, and arranging sheets on a dashboard. Use the official exam outline to find any skills you still need to practice.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Desktop Foundations Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or at a test center. Salesforce lists 40 scored questions, up to five unscored questions, and 70 minutes.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Questions may describe a small analysis task, such as comparing sales across regions or showing the top products, and ask which Tableau feature fits.
bestWayToPass: Know dimensions and measures: Dimensions describe categories or dates. Measures contain values that Tableau can summarize.
Learn the Marks card: Colour, Size, Label, Detail, and Tooltip control how a view displays its data.
Practice filters and sorting: Filter categories or values, sort by a measure, and choose whether a filter applies to one sheet or several.
Build a small dashboard: Combine sheets, add a filter, and test how a selection in one view affects the others.

certificationCard.description: This entry-level exam covers the basics of Tableau Desktop: connecting to data, building charts, filtering and sorting, writing simple calculations, and putting sheets together into a dashboard. The exam is 40 scored questions in 70 minutes, with a 48% pass mark, weighted towards Exploring and Analyzing Data (37%) and Sharing Insights (25%).

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Desktop Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Connect and prepare data
blocks.body: Tableau Desktop can connect to files, databases, and published data sources. A join combines columns from related tables; a union stacks rows from tables with a similar structure. A live connection queries the source as you work. An extract stores a copy in Tableau’s format and can support faster analysis or offline work. Tableau classifies fields as dimensions, which describe categories, and measures, which contain values to summarize.

blocks.heading: Build a view
blocks.body: Place fields on Rows and Columns to build a view. Show Me suggests charts that fit the selected fields. The Marks card controls how the data appears: use Colour, Size, Label, Detail, or Tooltip to change the marks. Measures are summarized by default, often as a sum, but you can choose another aggregation when needed.

blocks.heading: Filter, sort, and group data
blocks.body: Dimension filters keep or remove categories; measure filters keep values that meet a numeric condition. A Top N filter can show the leading products by sales. You can display a filter for viewers and set which sheets it affects. Sort data by a field or value. Groups combine field members, sets save selected members, and hierarchies let viewers move from a broader level to a more detailed one.

blocks.heading: Create calculations
blocks.body: A calculated field combines existing fields or values. You can use arithmetic, text and date functions, or IF and CASE logic. Aggregate functions such as SUM and AVG summarize rows for a mark. Table calculations, such as running total or percent of total, work with the values already shown in the view.

blocks.heading: Create dashboards and stories
blocks.body: A dashboard places multiple sheets on one canvas. Tiled objects fit into the layout; floating objects can be positioned freely. Dashboard actions make views interactive, for example by filtering one sheet from a selection in another. A story arranges sheets or dashboards into a sequence with captions. You can share finished work by publishing it to Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Desktop Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: These questions focus on everyday Tableau Desktop tasks. Identify what should change in the view or data, then select the feature designed for that task.

blocks.heading: Connect and combine data
blocks.body: Joins add related columns; unions add rows from similarly structured tables. Choose a live connection for current source data or an extract when a stored copy better fits the task.

blocks.heading: Build and refine views
blocks.body: Use Show Me to explore chart options. Put fields on the Marks card to change how data appears, and choose the right aggregation for a measure.

blocks.heading: Filter and organize
blocks.body: Use Top N filters for ranked results. Groups combine field members, sets save a selection, and hierarchies support drill-down.

blocks.heading: Use calculations
blocks.body: Use calculated fields for new values such as profit margin. Use table calculations for summaries based on marks already in the view.

blocks.heading: Share an analysis
blocks.body: Use a dashboard action to make sheets interact. Use a story when viewers need a sequence of views and captions.

sampleQuestions.question: A sales table and a returns table share an Order ID. You want return details beside each matching sale. Which data operation fits?
options: A dashboard action that filters the sales view
A calculated field that combines the two IDs
A join that matches the tables on Order ID
A union that adds the return rows below sales
sampleQuestions.explanation: A join matches rows on a shared field and brings columns from both tables into the data model.
whyWrong: A dashboard action filters views; it does not combine source tables.
A calculated field creates a value from fields but does not combine tables.
A union stacks rows rather than matching related records.

sampleQuestions.question: You have several monthly files with the same columns and want their records in one table. What should you use?
options: A group to combine category labels
A set to save selected records
A union to stack the rows
A join to match records by a shared field
sampleQuestions.explanation: A union stacks rows from similarly structured tables, which fits monthly files with the same columns.
whyWrong: A group combines members of a field, not table rows.
A set saves a selection of members.
A join matches rows across tables and adds columns.

sampleQuestions.question: How do dimensions and measures usually differ in a Tableau view?
options: Dimensions are always dates, while measures are always text
Dimensions break data into categories; measures are summarized values
Measures create categories, while dimensions are summed
Both types are interchangeable and behave the same way
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dimensions describe categories to compare; measures hold values that Tableau can aggregate.
whyWrong: Dimensions can be text, dates, geographic fields, or other categories.
This reverses the usual roles of dimensions and measures.
The two field types are used differently in views.

sampleQuestions.question: A scatter plot shows one mark for each region. You want one mark per customer but want to keep the same colours. Where should you place Customer?
options: On the Filters shelf
On Detail in the Marks card
On Colour in the Marks card
On Columns beside the region field
sampleQuestions.explanation: Detail adds information that can split marks without changing their visual colour.
whyWrong: A filter limits which records appear; it does not define the mark detail.
Colour would change the colour encoding.
Columns changes the view structure and may create a different layout.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager wants to show only the five products with the highest sales. What is the simplest approach?
options: Use a Top N filter on Product, ranked by Sales
Hide the other products manually after sorting
Sort the products and leave every product in the view
Filter Sales above a guessed value
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Top N filter keeps the leading members based on the selected measure.
whyWrong: Manual hiding must be repeated and may not update as data changes.
Sorting changes order but does not remove the other products.
A guessed threshold may return more or fewer than five products.

sampleQuestions.question: Dashboard viewers need to choose which Region appears in the view. What should you add?
options: A calculated field for every region
A visible filter control for Region
A group that contains all regions
A separate dashboard for each region
sampleQuestions.explanation: A visible filter lets viewers choose the region themselves.
whyWrong: A calculated field is unnecessary for choosing a region.
A group combines values but does not provide the required viewer control.
Separate dashboards are harder to maintain when a filter can do the job.

sampleQuestions.question: A Region filter should affect every worksheet that uses the same data source. What should you set?
options: Apply the filter to all worksheets that use that data source
Copy the filter to each sheet as a separate field
Place the filter on Detail in the Marks card
Convert the filter into a set
sampleQuestions.explanation: A filter can be configured to apply to all worksheets that use the same data source.
whyWrong: Duplicating the filter is harder to maintain and may lead to inconsistent settings.
Detail changes mark granularity; it does not set filter scope.
A set is a saved group of members, not a setting for filter scope.

sampleQuestions.question: Which calculation returns profit as a share of sales at the level shown in the view?
options: Use a Top N filter to rank products by profit and keep the leaders
Union a second source table that stores each product’s precomputed profit-to-sales ratio
Group the profit values into categories such as low, medium, and high
Divide aggregated profit by aggregated sales in a calculated field
sampleQuestions.explanation: The calculation SUM(Profit) / SUM(Sales) returns the ratio using the aggregation level of the current view.
whyWrong: A Top N filter selects ranked members; it does not compute a ratio.
A union stacks rows and does not calculate a ratio for the current view.
A group combines field members instead of calculating a ratio.

sampleQuestions.question: Several low-volume product categories should appear as one “Other” category. Which feature should you use?
options: A set that saves a selection for analysis
A hierarchy that adds drill-down levels
A group that combines category members
An extract that stores a data copy
sampleQuestions.explanation: A group combines selected members of a field into one category.
whyWrong: A set saves a selection but does not merge members into one label.
A hierarchy supports drill-down between levels.
An extract stores data; it does not regroup categories.

sampleQuestions.question: A source database is slow, and analysts need to work offline while travelling. Which connection type fits?
options: An extract stored in Tableau
A live connection to the database
A story made from the current worksheet
A union of the database tables
sampleQuestions.explanation: An extract stores a copy of the data in Tableau’s format and can be used offline.
whyWrong: A live connection queries the source and requires access to it.
A story presents views; it does not store the source data.
A union combines rows from tables but does not provide offline access.

sampleQuestions.question: A user selects a mark in one dashboard sheet, and another sheet should show only related records. What should you configure?
options: A data source filter that permanently removes records
A filter action between the sheets
A publish command for Tableau Cloud
A calculated field based on the selected mark
sampleQuestions.explanation: A filter action uses a selection in one view to filter another view.
whyWrong: A dashboard selection should not permanently remove source records.
Publishing shares the workbook but does not create the interaction.
A calculated field is not the dashboard interaction mechanism.

sampleQuestions.question: You want to guide viewers through a finding in a sequence, with a caption for each step. What should you create?
options: A story
A set
A field hierarchy
A dashboard with floating objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: A story presents sheets or dashboards in sequence and can include captions.
whyWrong: A set saves selected field members.
A hierarchy organizes levels for drilling into data.
A dashboard combines views but does not provide the same narrative sequence.

sampleQuestions.question: Viewers need to drill from Country to State and then City within one view. What should you create?
options: Three unrelated worksheets
A group that combines the countries
A hierarchy of the geographic fields
A measure filter on sales
sampleQuestions.explanation: A hierarchy lets viewers move through related fields from broad to detailed levels.
whyWrong: Separate sheets do not provide drill-down in one view.
A group combines members instead of creating levels.
A measure filter limits values; it does not create geographic levels.

sampleQuestions.question: A view shows total sales, but the user needs the average sales value for each order. Which setting should change?
options: Change the mark type from bars to lines
Change the field’s data type to a different kind of value
Rearrange the objects on the dashboard
Change the measure aggregation from SUM to AVG
sampleQuestions.explanation: Switching the measure aggregation from SUM to AVG changes the displayed value from a total to an average.
whyWrong: Mark type changes how data is drawn, not how it is summarized.
The data type defines the kind of value, not the aggregation.
Dashboard layout affects placement, not the value calculation.

sampleQuestions.question: You select several fields and want Tableau to suggest chart types that fit them. Which feature should you open?
options: The data source page to create an extract
The publish dialog to share the workbook
The calculation editor to write a formula
Show Me to review suitable chart types
sampleQuestions.explanation: Show Me suggests chart types based on the selected fields.
whyWrong: The data source page manages connections and data preparation.
The publish dialog shares the workbook.
The calculation editor is for creating fields, not suggesting chart types.
